extracted.intended_audience: engineers and readers interested in railway/locomotive history and early locomotive design
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and managerial criteria (design, boiler/steam management, trials, economics, and supervision) relevant to early locomotive construction and selection for public railways, as discussed in a historical account of the Stephensons. Emphasises steam-generation, draught, trial-demonstrations, costs, resilience, and hands-on engineering practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boiler arrangement and extension of heating surface
rubrics_metrics.description: "One of the most important considerations in the new engine was the arrangement of the boiler and the extension of its heating surface to enable steam enough to be raised rapidly and continuously, for the purpose of maintaining high rates of speed..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text links the locomotive's performance at high speed directly to the boiler's ability to generate sufficient steam continuously; guidance includes lengthening boilers and increasing the surface presented by flue-tubes to increase heating surface.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of steam depends on fuel and furnace temperature
rubrics_metrics.description: "The quantity of steam so generated, it will be obvious, must depend chiefly upon the quantity of fuel consumed in the furnace, and by necessary consequence, upon the high rate of temperature maintained there."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and operation must consider fuel consumption and sustaining high furnace temperatures as central to steam output; trade-offs between fuel use and steam production should be addressed in design decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of steam-blast to stimulate combustion (chimney blast)
rubrics_metrics.description: "He invented and applied the ingenious method of stimulating combustion in the furnace, by throwing the waste steam into the chimney after performing its office in the cylinders, thus accelerating the ascent of the current of air, greatly increasing the draught..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This steam-blast (exhaust into chimney) is cited as a major efficiency improvement (adopted c.1815) that quickened combustion and improved locomotive economy; it is a recommended mechanism to increase draught and fire temperature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to work heavy loads with speed, regularity and safety
rubrics_metrics.description: Stephenson pledged he would construct an engine "that should satisfy their requirements, and prove itself capable of working heavy loads along the railway with speed, regularity and safety."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key acceptance criteria for locomotive performance: capability under heavy loads, maintenance of regular schedules, and safety. Designs/demonstrations should show all three qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not proving an annoyance to the public (public acceptability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Directors authorised a locomotive to be prepared which, from the construction and experiments, "he is of opinion will be effective for the purposes of the Company, without proving an annoyance to the public."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond technical performance, social/public nuisance (noise, nuisance, safety perceptions) was a formal consideration; designs must minimize public annoyance to gain approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic efficiency: cost per ton and annual working charge
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting engineers computed "the cost of moving a ton of goods thirty miles by fixed engines would be 6.40d., and by locomotives, 8.36d.,--assuming a profitable traffic to be obtained both ways." They concluded fixed engines might result in lower annual charge despite establishment differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economic comparisons should consider both per-ton/per-mile costs and annual operational charges (not just initial establishment costs). Decisions may weigh longer-term annual charges and profitability assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential for future improvement (innovation potential)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters admitted "there appeared more ground for expecting improvements in the construction and working of locomotives than of stationary engines."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation frameworks should factor in the scope for technological improvement over time; higher short-term cost may be offset by greater potential for future gains through innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modularity and resilience to single-point failure
rubrics_metrics.description: Stephenson likened locomotive operation to "a series of short unconnected chains, any one of which could be removed and another substituted without interruption to the traffic; whereas the fixed engine system might be regarded in the light of a continuous chain extending between the two termini, the failure of any link of which would derange the whole."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference for systems composed of modular, replaceable units that avoid single-point failures; resilience and ease of substitution are explicit evaluation criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to demonstrate performance under specified trial conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The directors "determined to offer a prize of 500 pounds for the best locomotive engine, which, on a certain day, should be produced on the railway, and perform certain specified conditions in the most satisfactory manner."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adoption decisions were tied to public trial demonstrations against stated conditions; design validation must include successful, observable trials meeting explicit performance criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for practical convenience for public highway use
rubrics_metrics.description: Stephenson represented the greater convenience of locomotive power for the purposes of a public highway (contrasted with fixed engines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments include operational convenience (flexibility, ease of service) for public transport use — e.g., traffic handling, station-to-station serviceability — as a design criterion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make trials/experimentation before system-wide decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Stephenson repeatedly urged the propriety of making a trial of the locomotive before coming to any decision against it; the Board authorised an experimental locomotive as a result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional decision-making should require experimental trials of competing technologies before large-scale adoption; prototypes and demonstrations inform policy choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hands-on supervision and personal inspection of works
rubrics_metrics.description: Stephenson "took care to direct all their more important operations in person... one of his first duties in a morning before breakfast was to go over the various shafts... he would visit the extensive workshops ... and push them on with greater energy where needful... he examined the pay-sheets... To all these he gave his most careful personal attention."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective engineering leadership includes direct supervision, frequent on-site inspections, review of operational records (pay-sheets), and personal direction of key operations to ensure quality and progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training by principles and self-reliance (mentorship standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: He sought "to stimulate them to educate themselves--to induce them to develop their mental and moral powers... 'Learn for yourselves,--think for yourselves'... not so much to 'cram' the minds... as to bring out and invigorate the character of his pupils."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educational practice values teaching underlying principles, fostering independent problem-solving, perseverance, and character-building rather than rote memorisation; success measured by pupils' later professional distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear, terse, businesslike communication in reports and drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Swanwick recalled "the clear, terse, and vigorous style of Mr. Stephenson's dictation. There was nothing superfluous in it; but it was close, direct, and to the point..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical correspondence, reports and drawings should be concise, direct, and unambiguous; the author checked that amanuensis'd wording conveyed real meaning and corrected distortions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor in accounts and operational management
rubrics_metrics.description: On return Robert "instituted a rigid inquiry into the working of the concern, unravelled the accounts... and he soon succeeded in placing the affairs of the factory in a more healthy condition."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sound financial and operational oversight (rigid inquiry, account reconciliation) is treated as essential to sustaining engineering enterprises and enabling continued technical development.
